responses_by_run.answer: Athena turned Arachne into a spider as punishment for her pride and disrespect toward the goddess [1]. Arachne was a mortal weaver of extraordinary skill who refused to acknowledge Athena's superiority in the art of weaving [1]. When Athena, disguised as an old woman, advised Arachne to show humility and ask the goddess for pardon, Arachne scornfully rejected her and challenged Athena herself to a weaving contest [1]. After Athena won the contest and destroyed Arachne's web in anger at its perfection and its depiction of the gods' misdeeds, Arachne attempted to hang herself [2]. Athena saved her from death but transformed her into a spider, condemning her to dangle on a cord forever and to weave eternally as punishment for her presumption [3].

Prometheus was punished for two main transgressions. First, he stole fire and gave it to humans [1]. According to Apollodorus, when Zeus learned that Prometheus had hidden fire in a fennel stalk and given it to humans, Zeus ordered Hephaestus to bind him to Mount Caucasus, where an eagle devoured his liver daily [1]. Second, Prometheus attempted to deceive Zeus through a deceptive division of sacrificial portions at Mecone [2]. Hesiod describes how Prometheus tried to trick Zeus by presenting him with bones covered in fat while hiding the better meat [3], and notes that Prometheus 'matched himself in wit with the almighty son of Cronos,' which provoked Zeus's wrath [2].

Odysseus escaped Polyphemus through a two-part plan. First, he blinded the Cyclops by sharpening a wooden club, heating it in fire, and driving it into Polyphemus's eye with the help of his comrades [1][2]. When Polyphemus called out to other Cyclopes for help, they misunderstood his cries of "Nobody" and left him alone [1][2]. Second, after the blinding, Odysseus tied the Cyclops's sheep together in groups of three and hid himself beneath the largest ram, clinging to its fleece [1][2]. When Polyphemus opened the cave door to let his flocks out to pasture, he felt the sheep as they passed but could not detect the men hidden beneath them [1][2]. Odysseus and his surviving comrades thus escaped with the sheep to their ship [1][2].

At the wedding of Peleus and Thetis, the gods celebrated the marriage with feast and song on Mount Pelion [1]. The marriage took place after Peleus seized Thetis and held her fast despite her shape-shifting into fire, water, and various beasts, until she resumed her original form [1]. As wedding gifts, Chiron gave Peleus an ashen spear [1], and Poseidon gave him immortal horses named Balius and Xanthus [1].
